questions.q: What distinguishes a designed integration architecture from a collection of ad hoc point-to-point calls added one at a time?
options: The ad hoc approach is always faster to build and should be preferred for small orgs
A designed architecture deliberately plans how systems exchange data, rather than accumulating connections with no shared plan
There is no real difference; both produce the same long-term maintenance cost
A designed architecture never uses point-to-point connections under any circumstances
questions.explain: Integration architecture is a deliberate design discipline. Ad hoc connections added without a shared plan accumulate as integration debt, making each new connection harder and riskier than the last.

questions.q: A sales rep needs a credit-check result back in seconds, while a finance team's nightly reconciliation can tolerate a batch job running overnight. What design mistake does this lesson warn against?
options: Assuming batch jobs are never appropriate for finance data
Assuming real-time integrations are always more expensive than batch
Confusing urgency (how fast a response is needed) with business importance, as if they were the same axis
Assuming finance data is always less important than sales data
questions.explain: Urgency and importance are separate axes. A slow, overnight reconciliation can be just as business-critical as a fast credit check — the difference is how quickly a response is needed, not how much it matters.

questions.q: In this course's vocabulary, what is the difference between a payload and an endpoint?
options: A payload is the address a system exposes; an endpoint is the data being moved
They are two names for the exact same concept
A payload is the actual data being moved; an endpoint is the specific address a system exposes to send or receive it
A payload only applies to synchronous integrations, while an endpoint only applies to asynchronous ones
questions.explain: The payload is the data itself (a JSON body, a flat file). The endpoint is where that data is sent or received — a URL, a queue, a file location. They describe different things.

questions.q: Why do architects spend a disproportionate amount of integration project time on interface contracts rather than network configuration?
options: Network configuration is always more complex and time-consuming than defining an interface
Interface contracts are legally required documents in every Salesforce project
A vague or undocumented interface contract is where most real integration failures originate, while the network layer is usually the most reliable part of the chain
Network layers are typically unreliable and require constant redesign
questions.explain: The network is usually the most reliable link in an integration chain. Failures far more often come from a vague or undocumented interface contract — mismatched field names, unclear required fields, or undefined error behavior.

questions.q: A system is the source for one integration flow and the target for a different flow in the same org. Is this a valid design, per this lesson?
options: No, a given system must be fixed as either always a source or always a target across every flow
Yes, source and target are roles relative to a specific data flow, and the same system can hold different roles in different flows
No, only Salesforce itself can act as both a source and a target
Yes, but only if the system uses exactly the same endpoint for both roles
questions.explain: Source and target are defined relative to a specific flow of data, not fixed properties of a system. The same ERP, for example, can be the target when Salesforce pushes a new Opportunity and the source when shipment status flows back.
